meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Reflect upon your present blessings, of which every man has many; not on your past misfortunes, of which all men have some'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Dickens — from “A Christmas Dinner” in Sketches by Boz (1836), not A Christmas Carol. Wording confirmed against the primary source.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuine Dickens. It appears in his sketch “A Christmas Dinner” — first published as “Christmas Festivities” in Bell’s Life in London (December 1835) and collected in Sketches by Boz (First Series, 1836) — where the wording is confirmed word-for-word: “Reflect upon your present blessings—of which every man has many—not on your past misfortunes, of which all men have some.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: As “Christmas Festivities” in Bell’s Life in London, December 1835; collected in Sketches by Boz, First Series, 1836

source.excerpt: Dwell not upon the past—think not that one short year ago, the fair child now resolving into dust sat before you, with the bloom of health upon its cheek, and the gay unconsciousness of infancy in its joyous eye. Reflect upon your present blessings—of which every man has many—not on your past misfortunes, of which all men have some.
trail: The exact wording appears in Dickens’s sketch “A Christmas Dinner” — read the full text at Wikisource ↗.
The sketch first ran as “Christmas Festivities” in Bell’s Life in London (1835) before being collected in Sketches by Boz, per The Charles Dickens Page ↗.
It is commonly reprinted with “plenty” swapped for “many,” as on PassItOn ↗ — the original reads “many.”
source.excerptNote: The line closes a passage urging readers, at Christmas, to set aside grief and count what they still have.
source.rightsNote: Sketches by Boz was first published in 1836 and Dickens died in 1870; the work is long in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Charles Dickens
author.heading: About Charles Dickens
author.bio: Charles Dickens was the pre-eminent novelist of the Victorian age, author of Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol, David Copperfield and Great Expectations. Sketches by Boz (1836), a collection of his early journalistic pieces published under the pen name “Boz,” was his first book and predates the novels that made him famous.

misattribution.heading: The mix-ups
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Dickens is correct — but two smaller errors travel with this line.

items.why: Many collections file the line under A Christmas Carol because of its Christmas theme. It is not from the Carol; it is from the earlier sketch “A Christmas Dinner” in Sketches by Boz ↗.
Quote sites frequently print “of which every man has plenty,” as on PassItOn ↗. Dickens wrote “many.”

misattribution.truthLine: The thought — and these exact words — are genuinely Dickens’s, from “A Christmas Dinner” in Sketches by Boz ↗ (1836).

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The line comes from one of Dickens’s earliest published pieces, written before the novels that made his name. In “A Christmas Dinner” he sketches the warmth of a family gathering and pauses to counsel readers not to let old griefs spoil the present season — a gratitude theme he would return to, most famously, in A Christmas Carol eight years later.
